# Vector Databases at Scale

##### 340 ms became 4.1 seconds overnight

A legal-search product in Bengaluru ran nicely on 800,000 embedded case-law paragraphs, answering in about 340 ms. Then they onboarded a customer with an archive that pushed the corpus to 11 million vectors.

Latency went to 4.1 seconds. The Python process' memory climbed to 61 GB. Queries began timing out during business hours.

They had been using a flat index — brute-force cosine similarity against every vector. At 800k × 1536 dimensions that is a 4.9 GB matrix multiply, fast enough. At 11 million it is 67 GB, and the maths simply does not fit the machine or the latency budget.

Switching to an HNSW index with `m=32, ef_construction=200` brought p95 latency to 28 ms at 96% recall, in 14 GB of RAM. The vectors did not change. The search algorithm did.

Exact nearest-neighbour search is O(n·d) and does not scale. Everything in vector search is about approximating it well enough, cheaply enough — and knowing precisely what you traded away.

##### HNSW: navigable small worlds

HNSW (Malkov & Yashunin) is the dominant ANN algorithm, and the intuition is a skip list generalised to graphs.

Build a hierarchy of layers. The top layer contains a sparse random subset of points connected by long-range edges. Each layer down is denser with shorter edges. The bottom layer contains every point.

Search starts at a single entry point in the top layer and greedily moves to whichever neighbour is closer to the query. When no neighbour improves, it drops to the next layer down and repeats — coarse jumps first, fine refinement last.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph L2["Layer 2 - sparse, long hops"]
        A2((entry)) --- B2((n)) --- C2((n))
    end
    subgraph L1["Layer 1 - medium density"]
        A1((n)) --- B1((n)) --- C1((n)) --- D1((n))
    end
    subgraph L0["Layer 0 - all vectors, short edges"]
        A0((n)) --- B0((n)) --- C0((n)) --- D0((n)) --- E0((n)) --- F0((target))
    end
    C2 -.descend.-> C1
    D1 -.descend.-> E0
```

Complexity is roughly O(log n) instead of O(n). Three parameters control everything:

| Parameter | Meaning | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `m` | Max edges per node (layer 0 gets 2m) | ↑ recall, ↑ memory, ↑ build time |
| `ef_construction` | Candidate list size while building | ↑ index quality, ↑ build time only |
| `ef_search` | Candidate list size at query time | ↑ recall, ↑ latency — tunable per query! |

`ef_search` is the one to internalise: it is a **runtime** knob. You can serve interactive autocomplete at `ef=32` and a nightly batch reconciliation at `ef=512` against the same index, trading latency for recall per request.

Memory is roughly `n × (d × 4 + m × 2 × 4)` bytes for float32. At 11M vectors, d=1536, m=32: about 70 GB. That is why quantisation matters.

##### IVF and product quantization

**IVF (Inverted File)** clusters vectors with k-means into `nlist` cells, each with a centroid. At query time, compare against the `nlist` centroids, pick the `nprobe` closest cells, and search only those.

Rules of thumb: `nlist ≈ 4·√n` (so ~13,000 cells for 11M vectors), and `nprobe` from 8 to 64 depending on your recall target. IVF's characteristic failure is the **edge problem** — a query near a cell boundary may have its true nearest neighbour in an unprobed cell. Raising `nprobe` mitigates it at linear cost.

**Product Quantization** attacks memory rather than speed. Split each 1536-dim vector into `m` subvectors, run k-means with 256 centroids on each subspace, and store only the centroid IDs — one byte per subvector.

```
Original:  1536 dims × 4 bytes            = 6144 bytes
PQ (m=96): 96 subvectors × 1 byte          = 96 bytes     → 64× compression
```

Distances are computed via precomputed lookup tables, so it is fast as well as small. The cost is recall — typically 85–92% versus flat. The standard production recipe is `IVF_PQ` with a **rescoring** pass: retrieve 5× the candidates using compressed vectors, then re-rank those with the full-precision originals fetched from disk. You get most of PQ's memory saving with near-flat recall.

**Scalar quantization** (float32 → int8) is the underrated middle ground: 4× smaller, typically 1–2% recall loss, and almost no tuning. Try it before PQ. **Binary quantization** (1 bit per dimension) gives 32× compression with Hamming-distance search, and works surprisingly well with rescoring on modern embedding models.

| Index | Build | Memory | Recall | Query | Use when |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Flat | Instant | 100% | 100% | O(n) | Under ~100k vectors |
| HNSW | Slow | 130% | 95–99% | O(log n) | Default above 100k |
| IVF_FLAT | Medium | 100% | 90–97% | Fast | Large, memory available |
| IVF_PQ | Medium | ~2% | 85–95% | Fastest | 100M+ vectors |
| HNSW + SQ8 | Slow | ~33% | 94–98% | O(log n) | Best practical balance |

##### Choosing a vector database

| | pgvector | Qdrant | Milvus | Weaviate | Pinecone |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model | Postgres extension | Standalone (Rust) | Distributed (Go/C++) | Standalone (Go) | Managed SaaS |
| Best scale | < 10M | 10M–500M | 1B+ | 10M–200M | Any (managed) |
| Filtering | SQL, full power | Excellent, pre-filter | Good | Good | Adequate |
| Hybrid search | tsvector + pgvector | Native sparse vectors | Native | Native BM25 | Sparse-dense |
| Ops cost | Zero if you have PG | Low | High | Medium | None (₹₹₹) |

The advice that saves the most pain: **if you already run Postgres and have under about 10 million vectors, use pgvector.** Transactional consistency between your documents and their embeddings, one backup strategy, one set of credentials, one thing to monitor. Teams routinely adopt a dedicated vector database at 200k vectors and regret the operational overhead.

```sql
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  doc_id      text NOT NULL,
  department  text NOT NULL,
  updated_at  timestamptz NOT NULL,
  content     text NOT NULL,
  embedding   vector(1536) NOT NULL
);

CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (m = 32, ef_construction = 200);
CREATE INDEX ON chunks (department, updated_at);

SET hnsw.ef_search = 100;    -- per-session recall/latency knob

SELECT id, content, 1 - (embedding <=> $1) AS similarity
FROM chunks
WHERE department = 'legal' AND updated_at > now() - interval '2 years'
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
LIMIT 20;
```

##### Metadata filtering: the hard part

Filtering seems trivial and is where most vector-search systems break. Three strategies:

**Post-filtering** — retrieve top-k, then filter. Catastrophic when the filter is selective: search top-100 for `department='legal'` when legal is 2% of the corpus, and you may get two results back.

**Pre-filtering** — apply the filter first, then search only the matching subset. Correct results, but a graph index cannot be traversed on an arbitrary subset without either brute-forcing the subset or losing connectivity.

**Filtered ANN** — evaluate the filter *during* graph traversal, only following edges to nodes that pass. This is what Qdrant and Milvus implement, and it is the right answer. Qdrant additionally builds extra graph links for high-cardinality payload fields so the filtered subgraph stays navigable.

```python
from qdrant_client import QdrantClient, models

client.create_payload_index("chunks", "department",
                            field_schema=models.PayloadSchemaType.KEYWORD)

hits = client.query_points(
    collection_name="chunks",
    query=query_vector,
    query_filter=models.Filter(must=[
        models.FieldCondition(key="department", match=models.MatchValue(value="legal")),
        models.FieldCondition(key="updated_at",
                              range=models.DatetimeRange(gte="2024-01-01T00:00:00Z")),
    ]),
    limit=20,
    search_params=models.SearchParams(hnsw_ef=128, exact=False),
    with_payload=True,
).points
```

Index every field you filter on. An unindexed payload filter forces a full scan and undoes the entire point of the ANN index.

##### Sharding and scaling

Scale up before you scale out — a single machine with 256 GB of RAM handles 100M+ quantised vectors comfortably, and distribution costs real complexity.

When you must distribute, two axes:

**Replication** for read throughput and availability. Every replica holds the full index; queries load-balance. Simple, and usually the right first move.

**Sharding** for capacity. Split vectors across nodes, query all shards, merge results. Two schemes: **random sharding** (even load, must query every shard, merge top-k) and **semantic sharding** by tenant or category (query only relevant shards — far cheaper, but risks hot shards).

Multi-tenancy deserves a specific note: do **not** create one collection per tenant if you have thousands of tenants. Each collection carries index overhead. Use a single collection with an indexed `tenant_id` payload field and filtered search — Qdrant explicitly documents this pattern, and it scales to hundreds of thousands of tenants.

##### Embedding lifecycle management

The operational problem nobody plans for: **you will change embedding models**, and embeddings from different models are mutually meaningless. Cosine similarity between an `ada-002` vector and a `bge-m3` vector is noise.

Consequences to design for from day one:

- **Version everything.** Store `embedding_model` and `embedding_version` on every vector. Never mix versions in one search.
- **Reindexing is a migration.** Re-embedding 11 million chunks costs real money and hours. Plan a blue-green swap: build the new collection alongside, validate recall on a golden set, switch the alias atomically, keep the old one for rollback.
- **Incremental updates.** Deletions in HNSW are usually tombstones, so heavy churn degrades the graph and requires periodic compaction. Monitor deleted-vector ratio.
- **Cache embeddings by content hash.** Re-embedding unchanged text on every pipeline run is the most common source of wasted API spend.
- **Normalise once.** If you use cosine, L2-normalise at write time and use inner product at query time — it is strictly faster and avoids per-query normalisation.

##### Benchmarking honestly

```python
import numpy as np, time

def recall_at_k(approx_ids, exact_ids, k=10):
    return np.mean([len(set(a[:k]) & set(e[:k])) / k
                    for a, e in zip(approx_ids, exact_ids)])

def bench(search_fn, queries, warmup=50):
    for q in queries[:warmup]:
        search_fn(q)
    lat = []
    for q in queries:
        t0 = time.perf_counter(); search_fn(q); lat.append((time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000)
    return {"p50": np.percentile(lat, 50), "p95": np.percentile(lat, 95),
            "p99": np.percentile(lat, 99), "qps": 1000 / np.mean(lat)}
```

Compute ground truth once with a flat index. Then sweep `ef_search` (or `nprobe`) and plot recall against p95 latency — that curve *is* the answer to "which index should I use", and it is specific to your data, your dimensionality and your hardware. Benchmark at production corpus size and with production concurrency; a single-threaded benchmark on 100k vectors tells you nothing about 11M under 50 concurrent users.

##### Common mistakes

- A flat index in production, working fine until it suddenly does not.
- Post-filtering with a selective filter, returning almost nothing.
- Unindexed payload fields used in filters, forcing full scans.
- Tuning `ef_construction` at query time — it only affects build.
- Comparing vectors from different embedding models.
- No `embedding_version` field, making migration impossible to do safely.
- One collection per tenant at thousands of tenants.
- Benchmarking without warmup, or without measuring recall alongside latency.
- Jumping to PQ before trying int8 scalar quantization.
- Adopting a distributed vector database at 500k vectors when pgvector would do.

##### Hands-on

Load at least one million embeddings into a vector database. Compute exact ground truth for 500 queries with a flat index, then build HNSW and IVF indexes and sweep their runtime parameters, plotting recall@10 against p95 latency for both on one chart. Add a selective metadata filter (under 5% of the corpus) and demonstrate the difference between post-filtering and native filtered search. Measure index memory in each configuration.

For the mini-project, build a scalable semantic search service: a chosen vector database with a tuned index, indexed metadata filters, hybrid dense+sparse retrieval, embedding version tracking, a content-hash cache to avoid re-embedding, and a documented blue-green reindexing procedure. Load-test it at production concurrency and publish a benchmark report covering recall, p50/p95/p99 latency, QPS, memory and cost per million vectors. Then write your HNSW explanation — the layered graph, greedy descent, and the concrete recall-versus-speed trade that `ef_search` controls.

##### Key takeaways

- Exact search is O(n·d) and stops working; every ANN index trades a measurable amount of recall for a large speedup.
- HNSW's layered graph gives O(log n) search, and `ef_search` is a per-query runtime dial between recall and latency.
- Quantise before you distribute: int8 first, then PQ with rescoring, before you reach for a cluster.
- Filtering must happen *during* traversal — post-filtering breaks silently on selective predicates.
- Version your embeddings and plan reindexing as a blue-green migration; changing models invalidates every vector you have.
